title: Fractional & Small Interests
metaTitle: Selling a Small Fractional Mineral Interest in North Dakota
metaDescription: Own a tiny undivided sliver of Bakken minerals split among cousins and heirs? Here is why small fractional interests are still worth selling right.
heroLead: Our own family deed, by the time it worked its way through two generations, had shrunk down to a fraction with more zeroes after the decimal than digits in front of it, and we weren't the only ones on that section.
intro: A fractional mineral interest is simply an undivided piece of a larger tract that has been split among heirs, often over two or three generations, without the underlying land ever being physically divided. It's common across the Bakken and Three Forks counties, where an original 1930s or 1940s homestead deed got passed to children, then grandchildren, then great-grandchildren, and now a single 160-acre tract might have a dozen or more owners each holding a small fraction of it. Your royalty check might read something like a hundredth or a thousandth of the total, and it can feel too small to bother with.
It isn't. Small doesn't mean worthless, it just means the math has to be done carefully, and the paperwork trail has to be clean before a buyer can move on it.

sections.heading: Why interests end up this fractured
paragraphs: North Dakota inheritance law generally divides mineral interests equally among heirs when there is no will, and even with a will, families often split minerals the same way they split farmland, among all the children rather than to a single successor. Each generation multiplies the number of owners and shrinks each individual share, so a great-grandchild today might hold an interest expressed as a fraction of a fraction of a fraction under a single quarter section.

Operators track every one of these owners for division order purposes, no matter how small the decimal, which is why you may still get a check even if it only amounts to a few dollars a month. The interest is real property regardless of the size of the check.

sections.heading: The paperwork problem small interests create
paragraphs: The biggest obstacle for a fractional owner usually isn't value, it's proving the chain of title. If your interest passed down through probate, an unrecorded family agreement, or a will that was never formally probated in the county where the minerals sit, a buyer's title search can stall. Clean documentation, even something as simple as a certified death certificate and the original deed, moves things along faster than most owners expect.

If your interest was never formally probated and the original owner has been gone for years, that gap needs to be closed before a sale can close, and we can usually point you toward what a title company will need to see.

sections.heading: Selling a small interest without losing money to the process
paragraphs: Legal fees, courthouse trips, and drawn-out negotiations can eat a disproportionate share of a small interest's value if the process isn't kept simple. A straightforward cash purchase, where the buyer handles the title review and closing paperwork, usually preserves more of the actual value for a fractional owner than trying to run the sale through a full brokered listing built for larger interests.

It's also worth checking whether cousins or other heirs on the same tract want to sell together. Consolidating several small interests into one transaction can be more efficient for everyone and sometimes moves faster than each owner selling separately.

sections.heading: Tracking down scattered relatives before a sale
paragraphs: By the third or fourth generation, heirs to a fractional interest are often spread across several states, some in touch with each other, some not. A single title search at the county recorder can usually surface every recorded owner on a tract, which gives you a starting point for reaching out to cousins you may not have spoken to in years, even if the reason for reconnecting is a small royalty check none of you fully understood.

You don't need everyone's cooperation to sell your own individual share, but knowing who else holds a piece of the same tract can be useful information, both for understanding the full picture and for anyone who'd rather coordinate a single combined sale instead of several separate ones.

faqs.question: Is my interest too small to be worth selling?
faqs.answer: Rarely. Even a fraction of a percent under an active Bakken unit has value, and the transaction cost of selling a small interest is usually low if the paperwork is straightforward, so it's worth getting a number before assuming it isn't.

faqs.question: How do I even know what my exact fractional share is?
faqs.answer: Your division order or royalty statement will usually show your decimal interest directly, or we can help you work backward from the original deed and the number of heirs it was split among.

faqs.question: What if I never received a deed, just a royalty check?
faqs.answer: That can still be a real, transferable interest. We'll help you trace it back to the recorded deed or probate document that established it before moving forward.

faqs.question: Can multiple cousins sell their fractional shares together?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it's often simpler for everyone, since the buyer can review title once for the whole tract instead of running separate reviews for each small interest.
